title: TU Delft Achieves Direct Single-Atom Nuclear Magnetic Resonance via Scanning Tunneling Microscope Probe - Quantum Computing Report
gist: TU Delft researchers used ENDOR in a 0.4 K scanning tunneling microscope to drive the nuclear spin of a single 47Ti atom directly, published in Nature Communications. Working at fields up to 1.4 T suppressed electron-nuclear hybridization, preserving the nucleus's isolation from noise. This points to atomic-scale quantum memories and qudits, though gate control will still need pulsed sequences.

themes.theme: Direct single-atom NMR with an STM

insights.claim: Physicists at TU Delft's Kavli Institute of Nanoscience demonstrated direct NMR control of a single surface-adsorbed atom, a 47Ti atom on MgO, using ENDOR in a 0.4 K scanning tunneling microscope. It works without relying on electron-nuclear spin hybridization.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: This is a new tool for addressing individual nuclear spins as quantum resources.
insights.quote: achieving coherent nuclear addressing without relying on electron-nuclear spin hybridization
insights.locator: Physicists at Delft University of Technology’s

insights.claim: Nuclear magnetic moments are about three orders of magnitude smaller than electrons', which shields nuclei from environmental noise and gives surface relaxation lifetimes of seconds. Earlier STM approaches needed strong hyperfine hybridization at low fields (≤100 mT), which destroyed that isolation.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Avoiding hybridization keeps the long lifetimes that make nuclei attractive as quantum memory.
insights.quote: Historically, addressing single nuclear spins with an STM required strong hyperfine hybridization at low fields (≤ 100 mT), which mixes the states and collapses that environmental isolation.
insights.locator: Because atomic nuclei have magnetic moments

insights.claim: At fields up to 1.4 T, where electronic Zeeman energy dominates, the 47Ti nucleus could still be driven at 50–85 MHz, while the GHz electronic channel provided spin-polarized readout. Hybridization was suppressed about 10x.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Separating the readout and control channels is a building block for scalable atomic registers.
insights.locator: Because atomic nuclei have magnetic moments

themes.theme: Path to atomic-scale qudits and memory

insights.claim: The platform shows that atomic-scale nuclear qudits (here a six-level I = 5/2 system) can be integrated into engineered surface lattices. Full coherent gate control, however, will require pulsed-wave sequences rather than continuous RF driving.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: This is early-stage basic research, still far from a usable quantum memory product.
insights.quote: While full coherent quantum gate control will require pulsed-wave sequencing rather than continuous RF driving
insights.locator: Because atomic nuclei have magnetic moments
